brief.head: One fry fits all
brief.text: Industrial food ho­mogenises, Ajay Shah said, down to one potato for McDonald’s fries. “It is im­pos­si­ble to think deeply about the health sys­tem with­out think­ing deeply about the food sys­tem.” {012-C13}

brief.head: Islands of caste
brief.text: Ajay Shah com­pared India’s en­dog­a­mous groups to is­land ecosys­tems. Endogamy, said Amit Varma, cit­ing David Reich, left India “full of many dif­fer­ent thou­sands of small pop­u­la­tions”. {012-C10}

brief.head: Two tongues per boy
brief.text: Migrant men formed fam­i­lies with local women, so a boy spoke his mother’s tongue first, then the men’s. Amit Varma found that in Peggy Mohan’s *Wanderers, Kings, Merchants*. {012-R26}

brief.head: Brides on the move
brief.text: Outside elite cir­cles, Amit Varma said, women who marry and move al­most start from scratch. Chinmay Tumbe found that mar­riage is the largest source of in­ter­nal mi­gra­tion in India. {012-C11}

brief.head: Too warm to rise
brief.text: Dahi likes India’s heat, Ajay Shah said, but sour­dough needs about 20°C. Hence a cul­ture of un­leav­ened roti and naan, with khamiri roti the north­ern ex­cep­tion. {012-C14}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on where ‘Indian’ comes from
lead.head: A khichdi called culture

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 12

body: Amit Varma came dressed in a Patiala sal­war, and Ajay Shah asked him about the Indian look. Varma re­jected the label. Stitched cloth­ing came from out­side, he said, and his sal­war is of Middle Eastern ori­gin.

That set the theme. Almost noth­ing thought of as quintessen­tially Indian started here. Potatoes, chill­ies, toma­toes and guava came from South America. Marigolds came from Mexico; saf­fron prob­a­bly ar­rived via the Middle East; even idli fer­men­ta­tion may have come from Indonesia.

“You can make the nar­row ar­gu­ment that noth­ing is re­ally Indian so we shouldn’t call any­thing Indian per se,” Varma said. “But my broader ar­gu­ment would be that ev­ery­thing is Indian.” {012-C01}
Once in­flu­ences ar­rive, Varma ar­gued, they are ours. Language, food and clothes are at their best mixed: “The best things are al­ways a khichdi, a de­light­ful mix­ture.” {012-C02}
Even English counts. It bor­rows from Greek, Persian, Anglo-Saxon and Hindustani, Varma said, so it is an Indian lan­guage, and ar­guably not even an English one.
## Both ways

Trade al­ways ran in two di­rec­tions. Varma read from Pushpesh Pant’s *India: Cookbook*: “The traders brought with them the culi­nary se­crets of leav­ened bread, bak­ing, and noo­dles. In re­turn, the Indians in­tro­duced the Europeans to the joys of curry, man­goes and chut­ney.” {012-C03}
Shah’s favourite tale of the Columbian Exchange was the potato, which trav­elled from South America and, under Frederick the Great, re­shaped the lo­gis­tics of European armies.
## Sameness sets in

Mixing has a dark twin, ho­mogeni­sa­tion. Varma’s ex­am­ple, from the food writer Vikram Doctor, is the Cavendish ba­nana. India gave ba­nanas to the world; Latin America re­duced them to one dull yel­low strain and sent it back, and India’s own va­ri­eties are dying out. {012-S03}

Weddings ev­ery­where, Pushpesh Pant com­plains, have one Punjabi stall and one chowmein stall. Shah blamed in­dus­trial food, which wants a sin­gle stan­dard prod­uct, and swore off bas­mati rice for good.
Mass media did the same to lan­guage, Shah ar­gued. Television and films gave America one stan­dard ac­cent, and the state’s pro­mo­tion of Hindi re­placed the di­verse Hindustani of 75 years ago.

Both hosts see the tide turn­ing. Varma pointed to Stage, which streams in Haryanvi and Bhojpuri; in a long tail, you don’t need economies of scale. Shah pointed to YouTube, where peo­ple “dis­cover Konkani shows”. {012-C06}
## Ours to remix

Varma’s model of a cui­sine has two stages: local con­di­tions first, from pro­duce and cli­mate to fuel, class and caste, then a mix­ture of out­side in­flu­ences. A rice short­age gave the South upma; cow dung’s slow flame made Indian cook­ing a mat­ter of boil­ing.
Shah pleaded for sav­ing in­her­ited knowl­edge, like his mother’s recipe for the dal Osaman, while it still ex­ists. But cul­ture, he said, must not be “a fly in the amber”.

Varma called cul­tural ap­pro­pri­a­tion an in­co­her­ent idea: “If it’s cul­tural, how can there be ap­pro­pri­a­tion?” Shah told how Rabindranath Tagore’s heirs in­sisted his works be per­formed as in his time, and called it a tragedy.
Culture, Shah said, is the soft­ware of Homo sapi­ens, and soft­ware can be rewrit­ten. Varma had a shorter def­i­ni­tion, which he pro­posed nam­ing the show after: “Everything is ev­ery­thing.”

second.label: Food and labour
second.head: Upma, a wartime truce
second.deck: Amit Varma relays Krish Ashok’s theory of rice, rotis and women’s time

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the origin of upma

body: Krish Ashok has a the­ory, Amit Varma said, about why more women worked and more girls went to school in South India. Among many fac­tors, the South ate rice, cooked in one batch, while rotis took hours of labour every day. {012-S05}

Then rice ran short. Varma thought it was dur­ing the Second World War, around the Japanese in­va­sion of Burma. Orders came from above telling the South to eat more wheat, backed by wheat pro­mo­tion cam­paigns. {#wheat}

But the women were work­ing and the girls were at school, and no­body wanted to sit around all day mak­ing rotis. Their an­swer was a kind of wheat that cooks like rice. “And that is the ori­gin of Semolina Upma,” Varma said.

quote.text: So they came up with a com­pro­mise, which was a kind of wheat that can be cooked like rice, semolina.

third.head: High rents, safe menus

pic.caption: Amit Varma on why Bombay restaurants were bad

body: Five years ago, the food writer Vikram Doctor told Amit Varma that Bombay restau­rants were bad. The rea­son, he said, was rent. {012-S07}

“When you in­vest so much in open­ing a restau­rant, you can­not ex­per­i­ment with a niche or with some­thing ex­per­i­men­tal,” Varma said, re­call­ing Doctor’s an­swer. So the city got Udupi joints and pa­neer but­ter masala, which put Varma in mind of Pratap Bhanu Mehta, “be­cause he’s called PBM”. {012-J10}
Varma saw the same logic in Indian FM radio. Licences cost hun­dreds of crores and po­lit­i­cal news was not al­lowed, so sta­tions had no op­tion but Bollywood and pop­u­lar music. {#fm}
Had he pitched *The Seen and the Unseen*, or a show with “my friend Ajay Shah the card car­ry­ing econ­o­mist”, he said, they would have laughed him out of the room. Podcasting changed that.

p2.deck: How food, language and culture travel, mix and settle, as argued over by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

box.title: The food minds behind it
box.text: Pushpesh Pant sup­plied the pet peeves and *India: Cookbook*. Vikram Doctor, whom Amit Varma calls “the world’s best food writer”, sup­plied the ba­nanas, the marigolds and the cow dung, in *The Indianness of Indian Food*. {012-R02}

sections.label: From elsewhere
sections.head: Marigolds from Mexico
sections.caption: food that came from elsewhere
body: Almost ev­ery­thing we think of as Indian food is from some­where else, Amit Varma said, whether it is rajma chawal or tan­doori chicken. Potatoes, chill­ies, toma­toes and guava ar­rived from South America in what is called the Columbian Exchange. {012-C03}
Exchange ran both ways. In Pushpesh Pant’s ac­count, one of Vasco da Gama’s ship­ments alone car­ried fif­teen hun­dred tons of pep­per, along with gin­ger, cin­na­mon and cloves. {#pepper}

Vikram Doctor told Varma that the marigold, so com­mon at wed­dings, comes from Mexico. {#marigold} Saffron grows in colder cli­mates and prob­a­bly reached India via the Middle East; in India, only Kashmir has the right tem­per­a­ture for it.
## Wangi to egg­plant

When the writer Soity Banerjee recre­ated an Indus Valley meal, the only in­gre­di­ent we would recog­nise, as Varma re­mem­bered it, was bain­gan. What you call it, he joked, mea­sures your dis­tance from a Maharashtrian vil­lage. Say “wangi” and you are close; say “egg­plant” and you are fur­thest away. {#wangi}
Varma finds all this de­light­ful. Go back far enough, he said, and “even we came from Africa”.

~ He also told of the singer Bade Ghulam Ali Khan, fed only veg­e­tar­ian food by his hosts for days, who then sang as “but a shadow of him­self”. {#ghulam} Ajay Shah an­swered with George Bernard Shaw’s Caesar, on the bar­bar­ian who mis­takes his tribe’s cus­toms for the law of na­ture.

quote.text: He is a bar­bar­ian who thinks that the cus­toms of his tribe and is­land are the law of na­ture.
quote.who: George Bernard Shaw’s Caesar, as quoted by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The flattening
sections.head: The banana that ate the rest
sections.caption: the Cavendish banana
body: India gave ba­nanas to the world, Amit Varma said, retelling Vikram Doctor. Latin America re­duced them to one strain, the yel­low Cavendish, which Varma called “bor­ing, mo­not­o­nous, dull”, and sent it back. {012-S03}
The Cavendish won on economies of scale and shelf life. But India’s hun­dreds of in­dige­nous ba­nanas are dying out, Doctor laments, and food di­ver­sity is under threat.

Pushpesh Pant finds the same at wed­dings, with one Punjabi stall and one chowmein stall. Yet often, Varma said, within two square kilo­me­tres you can find six kinds of biryani, born of six dif­fer­ent cuisines. {#biryani}
## Why Varma wor­ries no more

The first burst of mar­kets, he said, brings a drive to­wards scale and same­ness. But deeper mar­kets and de­cen­tral­is­ing tech­nol­ogy now allow a long tail, in food as in Stage’s Haryanvi and Bhojpuri shows.

Ajay Shah, mean­while, has turned against bas­mati, the upper-class de­fault among thou­sands of Indian rice cul­ti­vars. Varma, al­lit­er­at­ing in Pant’s hon­our, called it “the bar­barism of bas­mati”. Shah went one bet­ter: “bru­tal­ity of bas­mati”. {012-J07}
~ In a pas­sage Varma read out, Pant pro­poses map­ping Indian food not by state lines but by sour­ing agent: tamarind or kokum, dried mango or vine­gar, star fruit or lime.

quote.text: And this to me has be­come like a metaphor for the dan­gers of ho­mog­e­niza­tion.

sections.label: Tongues and towers
sections.head: A dialect with a navy
sections.caption: language, mass media and architecture
body: When radio, tele­vi­sion and films ar­rived, Ajay Shah said, “the beau­ti­ful het­ero­gene­ity of lan­guage did shrink at first”. Many im­mi­grant com­mu­ni­ties in America con­verged on one ac­cent, mod­ern stan­dard American English.

North India, he said, never had one Hindustani, only many di­alects: a lan­guage, after all, is a di­alect with a navy. {012-J15} A scant 75 years ago there was no Hindi, and its pro­mo­tion by the state flat­tened a people’s lan­guage. {#hindi}

Now the tide has turned. “Stage one of elec­tron­ics is the ho­mog­e­niza­tion of radio and TV, which is mass media,” Shah said. On the in­ter­net, peo­ple can find Konkani shows, though there are re­ally many Konkanis. {012-C06}
## Built to im­press

Architecture, he said, shows the same pull. Powerful peo­ple build im­pos­ing struc­tures to make the peas­ants bow. From first prin­ci­ples, a build­ing should suit the local weather, ma­te­ri­als and crafts­man­ship, and still change as tech­nol­ogy does. {012-C09}
Shah wants food judged the same way: local, sen­si­ble, healthy, and cre­ative rather than aping oth­ers.
~ Food cul­ture, he said, should not be a fly in amber. It should evolve with local con­di­tions, pref­er­ences and prob­lems.

quote.text: The more to­tal­i­tar­ian the regime, the greater their in­ter­est in im­pos­ing struc­tures.

sections.label: Accidents of history
sections.head: Fuel, teeth and tapioca
sections.caption: why every cuisine is contingent
body: A cui­sine, Amit Varma ar­gued, is built in two stages. Local con­di­tions come first: pro­duce, cli­mate, fuel, class and caste. Then the world pours in, and which in­flu­ences take over is a mat­ter of chance and mimetic de­sire. {012-C05}

His ex­am­ples piled up. American PL 480 wheat, shipped dur­ing India’s agri­cul­tural cri­sis of the 1960s, brought a lit­tle roti cul­ture to the South. {#pl480} A nawab with bad teeth, the leg­end goes, gave us the melt­ing ga­louti kebab.
In the mid­dle of the nine­teenth cen­tury, short of rice, the king of Travancore saw that kappa, or tapi­oca, was a cheap source of starch. {#kappa} It be­came part of Kerala’s food cul­ture.
## The flame de­cides

Fuel mat­tered too. Old India cooked on cow dung, Vikram Doctor told Varma, and cow dung burns with a low, slow flame, so Indian cui­sine was built around boil­ing. Tandoors and fry­ing came with the Mughals. {012-S06}
Varma added that this is an­other rea­son the cow is ven­er­ated, which shows how much even re­li­gion is cir­cum­stan­tial.

~ Caste split kitchens as well. In the same vil­lage, Naren Shenoy ob­served, Brahmins and Dalits eat very dif­fer­ent food. A lot of great non-vegetarian food, Varma added, is eaten lower down the caste lad­der.

quote.text: So again, just how some­thing as sim­ple as what is your fuel source can shape an en­tire cui­sine.

sections.label: Culture as party
sections.head: Rabindra rap, anyone?
sections.caption: why culture can’t be appropriated
body: “If it’s cul­tural, how can there be ap­pro­pri­a­tion?” Amit Varma asked. Culture is the meld­ing of in­flu­ences, he said, which makes the fash­ion­able phrase cul­tural ap­pro­pri­a­tion in­co­her­ent. {012-C07}

Ajay Shah told what polic­ing cul­ture costs. His friend Rajeswari Sengupta told him that after Rabindranath Tagore died, the own­ers of his in­tel­lec­tual prop­erty de­manded his works be per­formed ex­actly as in his time. {012-S10}
Shah called it a tragedy, “a cold and pes­simistic view of the pos­si­bil­i­ties of human cul­ture”. He is no friend of rap, he said, “but surely there should be a Rabindra rap sangeet”. {012-J11}
## Shakespeare, remixed

Varma was sure such a thing ex­ists. Shakespeare was never wrapped in cot­ton wool, he said, so ev­ery­one has dug into him: David Gilmour has per­formed *Sonnet 18*, and the rap­per Akala has rapped it. “Culture is all of us hav­ing a party,” he said. {012-R24}

~ Shah took the aca­demic view. Culture is all the learned be­hav­iour of Homo sapi­ens, the soft­ware atop the hard­ware, shared even by Japanese mon­keys that learnt to wash sand from their rice. Software can be in­ter­ro­gated and rewrit­ten. {012-C12}

quote.text: Everything that is the soft­ware about Homo sapi­ens is cul­ture.

portraits.caption: William Shakespeare
portraits.credit: Attributed to John Taylor, public domain

quote.text: So it is a plea for preser­va­tion. At the same time it’s not a conservative’s plea for stag­na­tion. It’s not a fly in the amber. I don’t want to glo­rify the past.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A fish, a crop, a dal and a dialect, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how a Norwegian glut conquered Japan
stories.head: Something fishy about sushi
body: If Amit Varma or­ders sushi, salmon is his de­fault. It feels quintessen­tially Japanese. “But the truth is that salmon sushi as a con­cept did not exist till the nine­teen eight­ies,” he said. {012-S01}
Norway was har­vest­ing more salmon than it could store and needed ex­port mar­kets. So it sent a man named Bjorn Erik Olsen to Japan to meet the fish­ery com­pa­nies.
The Japanese were not keen. The salmon was too pink, not red enough. Local salmon was as­so­ci­ated with par­a­sites. An ad­ver­tis­ing cam­paign about Norway’s pure wa­ters did not work.

Varma, as a sto­ry­teller, imag­ined the glut spilling into the streets: class­rooms so full of salmon that chil­dren couldn’t go to school, po­lice sta­tions so full that law and order broke down. A “salmon max­i­mizer”, he called it, like the fa­mous pa­per­clip thought ex­per­i­ment. {#maximizer}

Olsen tried one final, des­per­ate tac­tic. He went to the food com­pany Nichirei and of­fered it some­thing like 5,000 or 50,000 tons of salmon, Varma for­got which, at a re­ally cheap price, on con­di­tion that it be sold as sushi. {#tons}

Nichirei’s rea­son­ing, in Varma’s telling: “Who can say no to cheap fish?” It took off. Mild salmon, the the­ory goes, was the sushi most palat­able to Western tastes, and this be­came the point at which sushi went global.
~ Norway’s salmon was saved, the chil­dren went back to school, and Japanese sushi was pop­u­larised. Ramen, Varma added, is also rel­a­tively re­cent.
stories.why: Dishes that feel an­cient are often re­cent ac­ci­dents of trade. A Norwegian stor­age prob­lem made a Japanese dish global, and Varma said it helped Japan as well. Look closely, he said, and pretty much all Indian food is the same. {012-S01}
stories.postscript: Varma apol­o­gised to Norwegian view­ers for any mis­pro­nun­ci­a­tion. He pro­nounces even Indian and English words wrong, he said, “which are ac­tu­ally the same”.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Norway’s salmon sushi

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Frederick the Great and the potato
stories.head: Guard it, and they will steal
body: Grain, Ajay Shah said, cit­ing James C. Scott, is calo­rie-dense, storable and easy to seize, and Europe’s ma­raud­ing armies grabbed it from vil­lages. {012-C04} The young Frederick the Great no­ticed that vil­lagers with pota­toes did bet­ter. The crop grows un­der­ground and looks dirty, and peas­ants left it in the soil, so armies ig­nored it.

As king, he pushed the crop, but peas­ants scorned the night­shade. So, in a story Shah al­lowed may be apoc­ryphal, Frederick planted pota­toes in heav­ily guarded royal gar­dens and told the sol­diers to look away when peo­ple came to steal them.
“This is the best way to make some­thing work,” Shah said. “It is to an­nounce that it is il­le­gal.” {012-S02} Hence, he added, cryptocurrency’s great fu­ture in India. {012-J04}
~ In some cases, Shah said, the potato shaped the out­comes of Frederick’s later wars.
stories.why: A crop that is hum­ble and hard to see can be a de­fence against plun­der. And mak­ing some­thing look for­bid­den, Shah sug­gested, can work bet­ter than or­der­ing peo­ple to do it.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma called it a bril­liant play of in­cen­tives, and urged ev­ery­one to read Scott’s *Against the Grain*. {012-R10}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Frederick the Great’s potatoes

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a family recipe that lives only in hands
stories.head: The dal the internet forgot
body: Ajay Shah is half Kutchi and half Kathiawari. Kutchis, he said, will proudly tell you they speak their own lan­guage, and many Gujaratis would not fol­low an au­then­tic Kathiawari con­ver­sa­tion.

One tiny sub­set of Kutchis makes a dal called Osaman, which Shah con­sid­ers one of the world’s great dals. He has searched the en­tire in­ter­net for his mother’s ver­sion. {012-S08} It isn’t there.
So he and his sis­ter plan to film her mak­ing it, and he asked the show’s pro­ducer, Vartika, on air whether she would take it on.
~ This was a plea for preser­va­tion, Shah said, not for stag­na­tion: save the knowl­edge while you can, then get back to in­no­vat­ing with it. {012-C08}

quote.text: There are some phys­i­cal mo­tions that she does that can’t be de­scribed and it’s just mag­i­cal how that thing hap­pens.

stories.postscript: Amit Varma re­called Bombay Canteen ask­ing peo­ple to mail in their grandmothers’ recipes, then serv­ing them as a day’s menu.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his mother’s Osaman

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Vinay Singhal and the shame of dialect
stories.head: No longer lost in translation
body: Vinay Singhal grew up speak­ing Haryanvi in a vil­lage in Haryana. When he joined a school in town in the ninth stan­dard, Amit Varma said, he found he didn’t know English, and had to learn it from scratch.

Then he moved to a proper big city, and found he had to learn Hindi too. Varma sees the pat­tern in Maithili and Bhojpuri as well: “The giant mon­ster of Hindi just tak­ing over, de­stroy­ing you.” {#monster}
Now Singhal’s plat­form, Stage, streams shows in Haryanvi and other di­alects. Kids who watch them come to him with tears in their eyes. {012-S09}
~ Varma called it ut­terly beau­ti­ful. It is also why he no longer frets about ho­mogeni­sa­tion: a long tail, he ar­gued, needs no economies of scale.

quote.text: For the first time in my life, I don’t have to feel ashamed of my lan­guage.

quiz.q: Which country’s glut of fish turned salmon sushi into a global dish in the 1980s?
quiz.a: Norway, which of­fered Nichirei cheap salmon on con­di­tion it be sold as sushi.

quiz.q: How did Frederick the Great, in one possibly apocryphal story, get peasants to grow potatoes?
quiz.a: He guarded royal potato gar­dens heav­ily and told sol­diers to let thieves through.

quiz.q: Which dish, by Krish Ashok’s theory, came out of a wartime push to eat wheat?
quiz.a: Semolina upma: a kind of wheat that can be cooked like rice.

quiz.q: Why, according to Vikram Doctor, was old Indian cuisine built around boiling food?
quiz.a: Its main fuel was cow dung, which gives a low, slow flame.

quiz.q: What, according to Chinmay Tumbe’s book, is the largest source of internal migration in India?
quiz.a: Marriage: women leave their homes, and often their whole lives, be­hind.

quiz.q: Which English word, Amit Varma pointed out, comes from Jagannath?
quiz.a: Juggernaut, which to Varma proves English is an Indian lan­guage.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 12. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Rabindranath Tagore (Generalstabens litografiska anstalt, public domain); Pushpesh Pant (Gazal world, CC BY-SA 4.0); William Shakespeare (Attributed to John Taylor, public domain); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); George Bernard Shaw (Bain News Service, publisher, public domain).

shelf.title: How The Desperate Norwegian Salmon Industry Created A Sushi Staple
shelf.creator: Jess Jiang
shelf.why: The full ac­count of how Norway’s salmon glut turned into the world’s de­fault sushi.

shelf.title: The Indianness of Indian Food (Episode 95 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Doctor
shelf.why: Vikram Doctor, whom Amit calls the world’s best food writer, on how Indian cui­sine is built from im­ported in­gre­di­ents such as the potato, the chilli and the guava.

shelf.title: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pushpesh Pant
shelf.why: A re­mark­able con­ver­sa­tion in which Pushpesh Pant urges Indians to ex­plore their own country’s food di­ver­sity, shar­ing the imag­ined maps in his head (re­gions mapped by their sour­ing agent) and how ‘clas­si­cally Indian’ in­gre­di­ents came from out­side.

shelf.title: We Are All Amits From Africa (Episode 343 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok and Naren Shenoy
shelf.why: Covers how cir­cum­stances such as rice short­ages and caste lines pro­duce dis­tinct foods.

shelf.title: A Scientist in the Kitchen (Episode 204 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok
shelf.why: Krish Ashok on the sci­ence and ori­gins of Indian food, with the story of a blind col­league who lis­tens to audio at 6x speed, Amit’s favourite ex­am­ple of how much the brain can adapt.

shelf.title: India: Cookbook
shelf.creator: Pushpesh Pant
shelf.why: Calls it a great book.

shelf.title: Cooking the world’s oldest known curry
shelf.creator: Soity Banerjee
shelf.why: As Amit re­calls it, the only in­gre­di­ent we would recog­nise today is bain­gan, which shows how lit­tle of our food is na­tive.

shelf.title: The Columbian Exchange
shelf.creator: Wikipedia
shelf.why: The back­ground to why so much of ‘Indian’ food is ac­tu­ally from the Americas.

shelf.title: Did Frederick The Great Introduce The Potato To Germany?
shelf.creator: Matt Robinson
shelf.why: Lets you dig into a story Ajay him­self flags as pos­si­bly apoc­ryphal.

shelf.title: Against the Grain
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how agri­cul­ture and grain-based early states made life worse for or­di­nary peo­ple, over­turn­ing the story of steady progress.

shelf.title: Caesar and Cleopatra
shelf.creator: George Bernard Shaw
shelf.why: Source of the line about the bar­bar­ian who mis­takes his tribe’s cus­toms for the law of na­ture.

shelf.title: Stage.in
shelf.creator: Vinay Singhal
shelf.why: Vinay Singhal’s ‘Netflix for Bharat’, stream­ing con­tent in di­alects like Haryanvi and Bhojpuri: Amit’s live ex­am­ple of tech­nol­ogy and long-tail mar­kets re­vers­ing the ho­mogeni­sa­tion of di­alects.

shelf.title: When and where do great feats of architecture come about?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Argues that grand struc­tures are a power move to make peas­ants bow, and that more to­tal­i­tar­ian regimes build more im­pos­ing ones.

shelf.title: Make Me a Canteen for My Soul (Episode 304 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Sameer Seth and Yash Bhanage
shelf.why: About pre­serv­ing food her­itage through mem­o­ries and sto­ries.

shelf.title: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Episode 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Singhal
shelf.why: Entrepreneur Vinay Singhal on build­ing Stage, a di­alect-first stream­ing busi­ness that proved scep­ti­cal VCs wrong and is push­ing back against Hindi’s pres­sure on India’s di­alects, in­clud­ing a ‘re­verse mi­gra­tion from Bollywood’.

shelf.title: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Naren Shenoy
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion with Amit’s friend Naren Shenoy, with a charm­ing ar­ranged-marriage story; Amit plans to re­search the caste and class roots of cui­sine with him.

shelf.title: Early Indians
shelf.creator: Tony Joseph
shelf.why: Tony Joseph uses the genes of liv­ing peo­ple to re­con­struct thou­sands of years of Indian his­tory: the first Indians, the Harappans, the Aryan mi­gra­tion, and how caste en­dogamy set in about 2,000 years ago after mil­len­nia of in­ter­min­gling.

shelf.title: Early Indians (Episode 112 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Tony Joseph
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Tony Joseph on the ge­netic his­tory of the sub­con­ti­nent, the audio com­pan­ion to Early Indians, in­clud­ing how India’s mi­grant groups mixed for thou­sands of years be­fore en­dogamy locked in.

shelf.title: Who We Are and How We Got Here
shelf.creator: David Reich
shelf.why: Reich ex­plains how full-genome stud­ies re­con­struct human his­tory and over­turned re­ceived wis­dom from ar­chae­ol­ogy.

shelf.title: Alice Evans Studies the Great Gender Divergence (Episode 297 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Alice Evans
shelf.why: Explores how main­tain­ing en­dogamy re­quires con­trol­ling fe­male sex­u­al­ity, which drives fe­male seclu­sion.

shelf.title: Mayabono Biharini (from BEDROOM)
shelf.creator: Somlata
shelf.why: Rabindrasangeet break­ing out of genre bound­aries: Tagore’s music doing what liv­ing cul­ture should.

shelf.title: Sonnet 18
shelf.creator: William Shakespeare
shelf.why: Shakespeare was never wrapped in cot­ton wool, so ev­ery­one has re­worked him, which is how cul­ture should work.

shelf.title: Sonnet 18 (David Gilmour performance)
shelf.creator: David Gilmour
shelf.why: An ex­am­ple of a clas­sic being freely remixed across eras and gen­res.

shelf.title: Sonnet 18 (Akala performance)
shelf.creator: Akala
shelf.why: Shows Shakespeare turned into hip hop.

shelf.title: Monkey Cuisine
shelf.creator: BBC Earth
shelf.why: Documents non-human cul­ture: an idea, not in­stinct, spread­ing from one fe­male to her band and then to other bands.

shelf.title: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants
shelf.creator: Peggy Mohan
shelf.why: Peggy Mohan reads India’s past through its liv­ing lan­guages, doing with lan­guage what Reich and Joseph did with genes: mi­grat­ing men mar­ried local women, so chil­dren spoke their mothers’ tongue first, and Sanskrit ab­sorbed local sounds such as retroflexes.

shelf.title: India Moving
shelf.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
shelf.why: Amit calls it one of the great books of the last ten years.

shelf.title: Understanding India Through Its Languages (Episode 232 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Peggy Mohan
shelf.why: Peggy Mohan’s lin­guis­tic his­tory of India in con­ver­sa­tion, the com­pan­ion to her book Wanderers, Kings, Merchants.

shelf.title: India = Migration (Episode 128 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Chinmay Tumbe
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion com­pan­ion to India Moving.

shelf.title: Varun Grover Is in the House (Episode 292 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Varun Grover
shelf.why: Amit’s con­ver­sa­tion with Varun Grover, who shares his idea of home as what­ever sur­rounds you wher­ever you are com­fort­able: your books, your room, the vibe.

shelf.title: Whole-grain sourdough bread
shelf.why: He calls it Pareto su­pe­rior to in­dus­trial yeast bread on taste and es­pe­cially on health.

shelf.title: Kefir grain (Kefirwala)
shelf.why: Good for your health and fun to ex­plore, even though its ideal 20°C fer­men­ta­tion tem­per­a­ture is hard to get in India.

laughs.text: Ajay tells half-Bengali Amit that some say the rasgulla’s ge­o­graph­i­cal in­di­ca­tor be­longs to Odisha and that the idea was brought by the Portuguese. Amit: ‘Sugar is poi­son, colo­nial­ism is bad, now we know why. Carry on.’

Ajay’s punch­line to Frederick the Great’s guarded potato gar­dens: ‘This is the best way to make some­thing work. It is to an­nounce that it is il­le­gal. So now you know why cryp­tocur­rency has such a great fu­ture in India.’
Ajay swears off bas­mati rice, call­ing it a tyranny. Amit, al­lit­er­at­ing in Pushpesh Pant’s hon­our, up­grades it to ‘the bar­barism of basmati’, and Ajay to ‘the bru­tal­ity of basmati’.
George Bernard Shaw’s Caesar and Cleopatra, quoted by Ajay: ‘He is a bar­bar­ian who thinks that the cus­toms of his tribe and is­land are the law of na­ture.’
Ajay uses the quip ‘a lan­guage is a di­alect with a navy’ to argue that pre-Independence Hindustani was re­ally many di­alects, flat­tened later into stan­dard Hindi.
